Materials per 100 sq ft: pitch 110 lb, coal-tar felt 45 lb, slag 300 lb or gravel 400 lb. Roofs of about 1/2 in/ft pitch on mobilization buildings may use asphalt or coal-tar built-up roofing
entries.use: Low-pitch roofs, nearly flat roofs where water stands
entries.how: Coal-tar pitch roofs must be mineral-surfaced; pitch not above 375 F
entries.dim: Pitch 30/25/55 lb per 100 sq ft (110 total); felt laps 19 in (17 in for 32-in felt); felt 45 lb; slag 300 lb or gravel 400 lb
entries.tm: Table C-8: 3-ply 20 MH per 1,000 sq ft
entries.wn: Do not heat coal-tar pitch above 375 deg F

entries.n: Reroof slate, tile and asbestos-cement roofs
entries.desc: Slate: replace entire roof if nails failed; 30-lb asphalt felt horizontally, laps not less than 3 in, turned up 6 in or more on vertical surfaces and over 12 in or more on ridges and hips, large-head roofing nails about 6 in apart; slates 20 or 22 in long for large buildings, 16 or 18 in for small; 3-in head lap; two large-head slating nails per slate, heads just touching the slate (don't drive home); bed slates in elastic cement within 1 ft of hips/ridges/rake edges; open valleys. Tile: same underlay; mission tiles (8 in wide x 14-18 in long, one nail, 3-in head lap), Spanish tiles (9 1/2-12 in wide x 12-18 in long, two nails, 3-in head lap), slab-shingle tiles (6-10 in wide, 15 in long, 1/2 in thick, two nails, 2-in head lap); nails long enough to penetrate at least 1 in into wood; eaves closures set back 3 in; mortar 1 part Portland cement : 3 parts fine sand; where hurricane winds expected lay tile in mortar. Asbestos-cement: same underlay; 2-in head lap; two large-head slating nails heads just touching; bed within 1 ft of hips/ridges; project shingles 1 in over gutter rear edges. Metal roofs: replace with nonmetallic materials
entries.use: Replacing old slate/tile/asbestos-cement roofing
entries.how: Restore the deck, underlay with 30-lb felt, 3-in laps
entries.dim: Slate head lap 3 in; asbestos-cement head lap 2 in; slab tile head lap 2 in; mission/Spanish tile 3 in; underlay 30-lb felt; felt laps >= 3 in; up 6 in vertical, over 12 in ridges; nails about 6 in apart; tile nails >= 1 in into wood; mortar 1 cement : 3 sand
entries.eq: Slating nails, elastic cement, roofer's cement
entries.tm: Table C-11 (pitch at least 3 in/ft) per 1,000 sq ft: asbestos-cement 35 MH wood purlins / 45 metal purlins; tile clay 55, metal 60; Table C-10: slate 55 MH
entries.src: TM 3-34.47 para 7-99 to 7-114 / Tables C-10, C-11

entries.desc: Step 1 nail down or cut off curled/warped shingles; remove or drive down protruding nails. Step 2 cut old first-course shingles at the eaves just below the butts of the second course and replace with a 1x3 or 1x4 strip flush with eaves line. Step 3 cut back gable-end shingles about 3 in and replace with 1x2, 1x3 or 1x4 strip flush with the gable end. Step 4 replace weathered ridge shingles with a strip of beveled siding thin edge down; treat hips the same. Step 5 fill open valleys with wood strips level with old surface. Step 6 inspect flashings; replace terne and galvanized flashings. Step 7 nails: 5d box or special overroofing nails, 14-gauge, 1 3/4 in for 16- and 18-in shingles; 6d, 13-gauge, 2 in for 24-in shingles; about 3 1/2 lb of nails per square of roofing. Step 8 apply per manufacturer
entries.use: Applying new wood shingles over weathered shingle roof
entries.how: Only if existing shingle roof can be made smooth and nailed properly
entries.dim: Nails 5d 14-ga 1 3/4 in (16-18 in shingles); 6d 13-ga 2 in (24 in shingles); about 3 1/2 lb nails per square; edge strips 1x3 or 1x4 (eaves), 1x2 to 1x4 (gable, cut back 3 in)
entries.tm: Table C-10: wood shingles 35 MH per 1,000 sq ft

entries.desc: Square off uneven sheathing and wrap heavy building paper around sides and top of the opening (no paper on the floor because the sill is worked into rough flooring); paper positioned even with the inside of the stud out to about 6 in on the sheathed wall, tacked with small nails. Rough openings are usually 2 1/2 in larger each way than the door (allows jambs, wedging and swing clearance). Example: 2 ft 8 in x 6 ft 8 in door needs a rough opening 2 ft 10 1/2 in wide (text truncated after width). No interior hinged door should swing against a natural entry, into hallways, or be obstructed by other doors
entries.use: Preparing the door opening before exterior covering
entries.how: Rough opening = door size + 2 1/2 in each way
entries.dim: Rough opening = door + 2 1/2 in each way; example door 2'8" x 6'8"

entries.desc: Batten door options: two diagonal layers at right angles (core for metal fire doors) or vertical tongue-and-groove/shiplap boards held by two to four ledgers (cross pieces), diagonally braced or not. Hasty method: several 2x6 boards; nail ledgers with edges 6 in from door-board ends; diagonal board between ledgers starting at the top ledger end opposite the hinge side to the lower ledger; on outside doors cover the weather side with roofing felt; nail wooden laths around edges and across the middle to hold the felt. Hang with T-strap hinges to door ledgers and hinge blocks on casing or post, leaving 1/4 in clearance around the door for expansion
entries.use: Hasty on-site door
entries.how: Several 2x6 boards with ledgers set 6 in from the ends and a diagonal brace
entries.dim: 2x6 boards; ledgers 6 in from ends; clearance 1/4 in all around

entries.desc: Mill-built doors: exterior usually panel type (stiles, rails, muntins, panels of wood/plywood/particleboard/louver/glass). Flush doors: wood frame with thin sheets on both faces; solid-core (better sound insulation, less warping, usually exterior) or hollow-core (lightweight, usually interior, cheaper). Specialty: double, sliding, folding
entries.use: Choosing doors
entries.how: Solid-core for exterior; hollow-core for interior

entries.n: Make and set door jambs and frames
entries.desc: Frame parts: head casing, jambs (head + 2 sides), sill (exterior only). Exterior jambs 1 3/8 in stock, usually rabbeted to receive the door; interior jambs 3/4 in stock with 3/8 x 1 3/8-in stops nailed on; rabbet depth 1/2 in. Hasty exterior frame: studs act as frame, studs 16 in o.c. with extra studs at sides of openings; casing set back width of the stud; 3/4 x 3/4 in piece over the door (set back the stud width) supports the drip cap; hinge blocks nailed to casing. Allow 1/2 in between frame and jamb for plumbing/leveling. Steps: cut side jambs to door height (less head-jamb rabbet depth) plus sill thickness and bevel, threshold, head jamb thickness, lug height; cut head jamb to door width less side rabbets plus dado depths, with 3/16 in door clearance; level floor across opening; cut side jambs from the dado lower edge by door height plus clearance under door, adjusting for floor variation; nail jambs to head through the dado with 8d common nails; set jambs with small blocks on subfloor as thick as the finished floor; plumb and level, wedge sides with shingles to studs, use a 5- or 6-ft straightedge inside jambs; check head and jambs. Jambs out of plumb make the door swing open or shut
entries.use: Door frame installation
entries.how: Plumb jambs, level the head, wedge with shingles, allow 1/2 in around the jamb
entries.dim: Exterior jamb stock 1 3/8 in; interior jamb 3/4 in; stops 3/8 x 1 3/8 in; rabbet 1/2 in; gap frame to jamb 1/2 in; head clearance 3/16 in; nails 8d common; straightedge 5-6 ft
entries.tm: Table C-5: door frames and trim – single exterior 3 MH, double exterior 3, single interior 3, double interior 4, sliding frame 4 (each)

entries.desc: Doors hinge to open in the direction of natural entry, outward in public buildings, against a blank wall, never into a hallway. Exterior doors use three hinges; interior doors use two. Steps: cut off stile extensions; plane stile edges so the door fits tight on the hinge side and clears the lock side by about 1/16 in, top fits square to rabbet, bottom clears finished floor by about 1/2 in; bevel the lock stile slightly; tack door in the frame and wedge at the bottom; mark hinge positions (slightly above lower rail and slightly below upper rail); use the butt as a pattern to mark gains; cut gains with a 1-in chisel and mallet; butts must fit snugly and flush; screw half of each butt to door and half to the jamb with pins inserted from the top; engage top hinge, then insert pins in bottom and center. Hinge setback usually 3/16 in. Install door closers per manufacturer instructions
entries.use: Fitting and hanging doors
entries.how: Three hinges on exterior doors, two on interior; 1/16 in lock side, 1/2 in bottom
entries.dim: Lock-side clearance about 1/16 in; bottom clearance about 1/2 in; hinge setback 3/16 in; 3 hinges exterior, 2 interior; 1-in chisel
entries.tm: Table C-5: fit/hang/lock – single exterior 5 MH, double exterior 8, single interior 5, double interior 7, screen doors 2; deduct 25% with power plane, hinge butt router and lock mortiser

entries.desc: Stops for single-piece jambs generally 1/2 in thick x 2 in wide, butt joint at head/side jamb junction, tacked until door hung; 45-degree bevel at the stop bottom about 1 to 1 1/2 in above finish floor. Casing 1/2 to 3/4 in thick, 2 1/2 to 6 in wide; margin 1/4 in from jamb edge all around; cut hinge-side casing square, then mitered top; nail from the top down with 4d finishing nails along the jamb side and 6d or 8d casing nails along the outer edge (long enough to reach studs); set nailheads about 1/8 in below the surface. Locks: cylinder locks for exterior (heavy duty), tubular/globular light-duty interior; mark lock position on lock stile 36 in from floor, mark case, knob hub and key positions and strike plate on jamb, bore and mortise, strike plate flush or slightly below jamb face. Panic hardware per manufacturer
entries.use: Finishing a door opening
entries.how: Casing set back 1/4 in from jamb; lock set 36 in above floor
entries.dim: Stop 1/2 x 2 in; bevel 45 degrees at 1 to 1 1/2 in above floor; casing 1/2-3/4 in thick x 2 1/2-6 in wide; margin 1/4 in; nails 4d and 6d/8d; set 1/8 in; lock at 36 in
entries.eq: Miter box, miter square, hammer, nail set, block plane

entries.n: Window frames, sills and hasty sashes
entries.desc: Window = frame (head, two jambs, sill) + sash. Double the studs on each side of the opening to form trimmers, insert a header (doubled and trussed if wide) and a rough sill. Hasty construction: simple openings with stops nailed to studs; sash hinged inside/outside or sliding; sliding sash with overlapping panes is most common in Army construction. Sill slope usual 1 to 5 in (per text), sill extends about 1 1/2 in beyond sheathing. Sliding sashes balanced by weights half the sash weight. Hasty sash: 1x3 stock with reinforced rolled plastic glass substitute; make two frames (glass substitute on one), nail together with joints staggered; don't make sash larger than the glass substitute (or add a muntin fastened with corrugated fasteners; center muntin for long sashes); side pieces cut to sash height less one material width; top/bottom pieces to window length less one material width; fasten joints with corrugated fasteners
entries.use: Framing window openings and building simple sashes
entries.how: Double the studs on each side; hasty sliding sash uses little time
entries.dim: Sash stock 1x3; sill projects about 1 1/2 in; sill slope 1 to 5 in (as printed)
entries.tm: Table C-7: double hung wood 4 MH each, casement single 4, fixed sash 3, jalousie 2, skylight 8, louver 5, screen 2

entries.desc: Window screen sash usually 3/4-in stock (1 1/8 in for large windows) and 1 3/4 or 2 1/4 in wide; cut screen 1 in wider and longer than the opening; rabbet inside edges about 3/4 x 1/2 in; attach screen in the rabbet and nail 3/8 x 1/2 in molding flush with sash face. Attach starting at one end, hold tight, hand-stretch along the sides with weave parallel to the ends and sides. Door screens: two frames – first frame of two side pieces as long as the door and crosspieces as wide as the door less the two side pieces (1x4 for sides and top, 1x6 for bottom and middle), joined with corrugated fasteners or triangular corner splices; second frame with crosspiece as wide as the door and sides cut to fit between crosspieces; second frame nailed over the first; two short 1x4 braces opposite the hinge side for push-pull plates
entries.use: Insect screening
entries.how: Cut screen 1 in larger than opening; copper staples for bronze/copper, cadmium for aluminum
entries.dim: Sash 3/4 in (1 1/8 in large); width 1 3/4 or 2 1/4 in; screen cut +1 in; rabbet 3/4 x 1/2 in; molding 3/8 x 1/2 in; door screen 1x4 sides/top, 1x6 bottom/middle

entries.n: Hoods or canopies for tropical screened openings
entries.desc: Short rafters framed to the end walls with knee braces; rafters nailed to the wall with bottom edge flush with the bottom of the end plate; rafters and braces 2x4 with 8d or 10d nails; sheathing same as roof sheathing, covered with roll roofing; hood extends about 2 1/2 or 3 ft from the building
entries.use: Tropical climates, end walls
entries.how: 2x4 rafters and braces, 8d or 10d nails; projects about 2 1/2 to 3 ft
entries.dim: 2x4 rafters and braces; 8d or 10d nails; projection 2 1/2 to 3 ft

entries.desc: Sheets: 4x8, 4x9, 4x10, 4x14, 4x16 ft; thickness 1/4, 3/8, 1/2, 5/8 in (1/4 or 3/8 for renovations over minor irregularities, not for single layer; 1/2 in most common, adequate for 16- or 24-in o.c. framing; 5/8 in recommended for single-layer walls and multi-layer fire-resistant). Always start with the ceiling, then begin walls in one corner and work around; joints break on stud/joist centerlines. Ceiling: first sheet measured from top plate inside edge to outside edge of second ceiling joist, 48 in long; nail spacing on ceilings 5 to 7 in o.c.; run sheet length across joists to prevent sagging. Walls: start where studs are on center and a full sheet can lie horizontally; no joints above or below door/window openings; place snug against ceiling, level, edges on stud centers; nails 6 to 8 in o.c., 3/8 in from edge. Receptacle cutout: measure from inside corner and from installed sheetrock, allow 1/16 in clearance all around; punch hole with utility knife, cut with keyhole saw using slight undercut bevel. Corner bead on exterior corners with crimper (or nails); it is nailed/screwed 6 in on center. Nails: oversized head, rust-treated (annular-ring most common); single nailing 6-7 in on ceilings, 6-8 in on walls; double nailing: pairs 2 to 2 1/2 in apart, pair centers about 12 in apart, outer edges 7 in o.c., 3/8 to 1/2 in from edge; no double nailing around sheet perimeter. Drive each nail slightly below the surface (dimple) without breaking paper; screws via power screw gun
entries.use: Interior wall and ceiling covering
entries.how: Ceiling first; joints on stud/joist centers; dimple nails without breaking paper
entries.dim: Sheet sizes above; nails ceilings 5-7 in (6-7), walls 6-8 in o.c.; edge distance 3/8 to 1/2 in; double nail pairs 2-2 1/2 in apart, 12 in between pairs, 7 in outer o.c.; corner bead 6 in o.c.; receptacle clearance 1/16 in
entries.eq: Sheetrock hammer, carrier/lifter, utility knife, T-square, keyhole saw, Surform, 4-ft level, saw horses, 16-ft tape, chalk line, corner-bead crimper
entries.tm: Table C-4: walls plasterboard (incl. tape) 48 MH per 1,000 sq ft; ceilings plasterboard 64 MH; for small rooms add 30-50 percent

entries.desc: Run a knife edge over nailheads – a click means a nail needs recessing. 4-in knife and mud pan: coat over nails; heavy coat over joint, center the tape, press in, remove excess without wrinkles or air bubbles; inside corners: fold tape lengthwise, press into compound with corner tool. First coat: medium coat feathered with 6-in knife about 2 to 3 in each side. Second coat (first coat dry): 4-in knife thin coat over nails; 6-in knife on joints feathered 6 to 8 in each side. Third coat (dry): 10-in knife (tool list says 12-in) feathered 10 to 12 in each side; nails normally don't need a third coat. Finish with damp sponge or fine sandpaper. Tapered sheet edges are 1/16 in thinner over about 1 1/4 in. Fiber-mesh tape is self-sticking (no bedding coat). Perforated paper tape is easier to bed. Corner trowel flexes 90 to 103 degrees
entries.use: After hanging, to make surfaces paint-ready
entries.how: Three coats feathered wider each time; check for nails that need recessing with the knife edge
entries.dim: Knives 4 in (tape/nails), 6 in (2nd coat), 10 or 12 in (3rd coat); feathering 2-3 in, 6-8 in, 10-12 in
entries.eq: Knives, mud pan, corner trowel, tape banjo, sponge, sandpaper

entries.desc: Small holes: fiber-mesh tape over the hole, compound, feather, sand/sponge. Fist-size: cut a rectangle around the hole with a keyhole saw; cut a 1x2 or 1x3 backing slightly larger than the opening, glue or screw it in; glue a patch to the backing with wallboard adhesive or mastic; tape, compound, feather, sand. Large holes: cut a rectangle reaching the centers of the nearest studs; screw or nail the patch to the studs; tape, compound, feather, sand
entries.use: Repairing holes
entries.how: Small: fiber-mesh tape; fist-size: backing 1x2 or 1x3; large: cut to stud centers
entries.dim: Backing 1x2 or 1x3

entries.desc: Plywood most common: 4 ft wide, 5-8 ft long, 1/4 to 3/4 in thick, usually vertical floor to ceiling; joints covered with battens or splines if desired. Fiberboard sheets 1/2 to 2 in thick, cut with a utility knife, attached directly to joists; cover joints with wood/fiberboard battens; tiles need furring strips across joints; lap-joint tiles blind-nailed or stapled; T&G tiles use 2d box nails through metal clips. Solid backing: furring strips at right angles across bottom of joists, short furring along joists, metal channels nailed to furring strips. Ceiling sheetrock: joints on centers of ceiling joists; use a brace to hold sheet while nailing; lengths across joists. Ceiling molding: coped inside corners; finish nails into upper wall plates and ceiling joist
entries.use: Interior panels as alternatives to sheetrock
entries.how: Plywood hung vertically floor to ceiling; fiberboard tiles may need furring strips
entries.dim: Plywood 4 ft x 5-8 ft, 1/4-3/4 in; fiberboard 1/2-2 in thick; 2d box nails for T&G tiles
entries.eq: Utility knife, brace for holding panels
entries.tm: Table C-4: walls plywood 32 MH per 1,000 sq ft; ceilings wood 48, cemented tile 32, panel with suspension 72

entries.desc: Square-edge (two-piece) baseboard usually 5/8 x 3 1/4 in or wider topped with base cap; one-piece ranch base 3/4 x 3 1/4 in or wider (and 1/2 x 2 1/4 to 1/2 x 3 1/4 in or wider); base shoe usually 1/2 x 3/4 in. Baseboard: butt joint at inside corners and mitered joint at outside corners; nailed to each stud with two 8d finishing nails. Base molding: coped joint at inside corners (first piece square cut, second coped by sawing a 46-degree miter), mitered outside corners; join several pieces with a lap miter. Nail base shoe into the subfloor with long slender nails, not into the baseboard
entries.use: Trim at wall/floor junction
entries.how: Butt at inside corners (or coped), miter outside corners; two 8d finishing nails per stud
entries.dim: Baseboard 5/8 x 3 1/4 in+; ranch 3/4 x 3 1/4 in+; shoe 1/2 x 3/4 in; two 8d finishing nails per stud
entries.eq: Miter box, coping saw, nail set
entries.tm: Table C-4: baseboard (2 member) 72 MH per 1,000 linear feet

entries.desc: Single-span bridge: supported only by two abutments; multispan has intermediate supports. Pile bent: highway only, vertical + lateral loads, spans up to 50 ft. Trestle bent: highway only, vertical loads only, spans up to 30 ft and ground-to-grade height up to 12 ft. Pile-bent pier (two or more pile bents with common cap): highway and railroad, vertical + lateral loads, spans up to 200 ft. Trestle-bent pier (timber trestle pier): highway only, vertical only, spans up to 60 ft and heights up to 18 ft. Crib pier (log-cabin style timber filled with rock): highway only, vertical only, span up to 50 ft and height up to 12 ft; should need no exterior bracing. Abutments are footing type (footings, sill, end dam) or pile type (piles, cap, sheeting)
entries.use: Planning a nonstandard fixed highway bridge
entries.how: Know the span and height limits of each support type
entries.dim: Pile bent <= 50 ft span; trestle bent <= 30 ft span and <= 12 ft height; pile-bent pier <= 200 ft; trestle-bent pier <= 60 ft and <= 18 ft; crib pier <= 50 ft span and <= 12 ft height

entries.desc: Longitudinal bracing stabilizes the centerline; transverse (sway/lateral) bracing gives stability at right angles. Diaphragms are braces between stringers; spacing ratio L/b (distance between diaphragms to width of top of stringer) should not exceed 30 for timber. Example: 6-in-wide stringer -> L = 30 x 6 = 180 in = 15 ft, so diaphragms every 15 ft
entries.use: Preventing lateral buckling of stringers
entries.how: Diaphragms: L/b not more than 30 for timber
entries.dim: L/b <= 30; example 6-in stringer -> 15 ft

entries.n: Lay out bridge centerline and abutment
entries.desc: Centerline: stretch a line or tape across the stream/ravine; attach to stakes driven at least 15 ft behind proposed abutment sills (intermediate stakes for defiles wider than 100 ft); place line at the intended top of flooring or a known distance above/below. Use the simplest abutment (often timber sill with timber footings). Place sill under the tape, square to the centerline by measuring from the centerline stake 15 ft behind to each end of sill (equal distances); mark and remove sill to build the foundation: level surface about 2 in above final position to allow settling; if over-dug, raise with planking, not earth; outside footings under sill ends, long dimension parallel to centerline; remaining footings equally spaced; sill centered on footings with largest dimension vertical; provide drainage. End dam installed after stringers and planks
entries.use: Starting a trestle-bent bridge
entries.how: Centerline stakes at least 15 ft behind the sill; sill square to the line
entries.dim: Stakes >= 15 ft behind sills; intermediate stakes if defile > 100 ft; footing surface about 2 in high for settling

entries.n: Retaining walls and trestle bent construction
entries.desc: Retaining wall: planks or logs supported by piles or posts driven 4 ft into the ground; wing walls prevent washout; anchor cables from pile tops to a deadman (not needed with two or three rows of piles driven as far as they go). Trestle bents: measure each span along the centerline from the abutment sill, drive a stake under the centerline at each bent center, excavate and place footings as for abutment; bent height = centerline-to-footing distance less deck, tread and stringer thickness (and nailing strips for steel stringers); post height = bent height less cap and sill thickness. Make cap and sill length = roadway width + 2 ft; outside posts under roadway edges 1 ft from ends, other posts evenly spaced; fasten sill and cap to posts with driftpins or bolts (scabbing for fast erection); nail transverse bracing (usually 3x12 planks) on both sides to each post, ends extending beyond nails to prevent splitting; raise the bent plumb and hold with temporary braces to stakes until permanent longitudinal bracing is nailed
entries.use: Abutment wing walls and intermediate bents
entries.how: Cap and sill = roadway width + 2 ft; outside posts 1 ft from ends
entries.dim: Piles/posts 4 ft into ground; cap/sill = roadway + 2 ft; outside posts 1 ft from ends; bracing 3x12 planks

entries.desc: Wood stringers extend across sills and caps and lap with next span's. Lapped: one outside stringer inside face under inside face of one curb, other outside stringer outside face under inside face of other curb; others spaced evenly (or grouped under vehicle tracks on narrow one-lane bridges). Butted or continuous: outside faces of outside stringers under inside faces of curbs. Fasten wood stringers by nailing diagonally through the side into the cap or by driftbolts (bore hole smaller in diameter and 3 in shorter than the driftbolt through stringer into cap). Steel stringers: railroad spikes in the cap beside flange; 60d nails partly driven into the cap and bent over the bottom flange; or nails/driftbolts through prebored holes in the flange; check frequently if not fastened through flanges; fasten wood nail strips to top flange for decking. Laminated deck may be fastened to steel with metal clips or partly driven nails bent around the flange
entries.use: Superstructure
entries.how: Wood stringers: diagonal nails or driftbolts with hole 3 in shorter than the bolt
entries.dim: Driftbolt hole 3 in shorter and smaller in diameter; 60d nails for steel stringer flanges
entries.wn: Frequent inspection needed if steel stringers not fastened through flanges

entries.desc: Decking: laminated (planks on edge; solid or open with uniform spacing) or solid plank. Open laminated deck with laminations spanning full width: two spacing blocks between laminations, spacers on the stringer nearest one-third of the lamination length; if laminations are too short (usually two-lane bridges) lap them on a central stringer with a spacer block at each outside stringer. Solid laminated: place laminations tight. Solid-plank deck: planks laid at right angles to stringers with 1/4 in space for swelling when wet; extend decking about 2 ft at approximately 5-ft intervals to support handrail posts. Tread: planks usually 2 or 3 in thick, various lengths, laid parallel to traffic over decking between (not under) the curbs; one-lane bridges tread only wheel/track path, two-lane fully covered
entries.use: Flooring a timber trestle bridge
entries.how: Solid plank: 1/4 in between planks; extend decking 2 ft every 5 ft for handrail posts
entries.dim: Plank spacing 1/4 in; deck extensions 2 ft at about 5 ft intervals; tread planks 2 or 3 in thick

entries.n: Curbs, handrails, sidewalks and end dam
entries.desc: Curbs: 6x6 timber on 6x12x30-in curb risers spaced about 5 ft o.c., bolted to decking with 1/2-in bolts, two per riser. Handrails: 2x4 or larger; over a laminated deck make posts and knee braces of deck material fitted between extended laminations; on solid-plank decks toenail 4x4 posts (or two 2x4s nailed together) to extended planks; posts 42 in high on 5-ft centers; at least 10 in from inside face of curb to inside face of handrail. Sidewalks: extend decking an additional 36 in, stiffener under the outside edge, braces to stringers where needed. End dam: built of flooring planks across the ends of the stringers from top of footing to top of tread after stringers and flooring are in; then finish approach up to deck level and post traffic-control and classification signs
entries.use: Finishing a timber trestle bridge
entries.how: Curb 6x6 on 6x12x30 risers 5 ft o.c. with two 1/2-in bolts each; handrail posts 42 in high at 5 ft
entries.dim: Curb 6x6; risers 6x12x30 in at about 5 ft; 1/2-in bolts x 2 per riser; handrail 2x4+; posts 4x4 (or 2x 2x4), 42 in high, 5-ft centers; handrail >= 10 in from curb; sidewalk +36 in

entries.desc: Bearing piles support framework and decking: straight, at least 6 in across the top, 18 in across the butt, 60 to 80 ft long; spaced center to center 6 to 10 ft in one direction and 5 ft in the other. Fender piles: placed about 2 1/4 ft out from the centerline of the outside row of bearing piles, about 18 ft apart, along sides where ships dock. Mooring piles: aligned with the outside row of bearing piles, about 30 ft apart, braced, extending about 4 ft above the deck. Treat timber piles with creosote or other preservative against fungi and marine borers
entries.use: Layout of timber-pile wharf
entries.how: Bearing piles 6-10 ft x 5 ft; fender piles 18 ft apart; mooring piles 30 ft apart
entries.dim: Bearing piles: top >= 6 in, butt 18 in, 60-80 ft; spacing 6-10 ft x 5 ft; fender 2 1/4 ft out, 18 ft apart; mooring 30 ft apart, 4 ft above deck
entries.wn: Timber piling must be treated with creosote or another preservative

entries.n: Straighten and cut piles; cap and brace bents
entries.desc: Straighten piles as soon as misalignment is noticed; if more than a few inches out of plumb, set true. Use block and tackle (with hammer impact), jet, or block and tackle with alignment frame; floating template may position piles from a floating driver. Cutting: butts left 2 or 3 ft above finished elevation; nail saw guides across all piles in the bent so the cap bears evenly. Capping: put cap in place, bore driftpin holes through the cap into each pile top and drive driftpins; at cap joints bolt a splice scab across to both sides. Bracing: bolt diagonal timbers to each pile, opposite diagonals on each side of the bent; for diameter mismatch hew/dap big piles, block out small piles with fillers, or use brace flexibility
entries.use: During/after pile driving
entries.how: Fix misaligned piles immediately; cut all piles in a bent with saw guides
entries.dim: Pile butts 2 or 3 ft above final elevation
entries.eq: Block and tackle, jet, alignment frame, floating template, saw guides, driftpins, bolts
entries.tm: Table C-12 (4x10x4-ft bracing members): horizontal brace 1.0 MH each, diagonal 0.8; capping per 1,000 sq ft – wood 100 MH, steel 150, concrete 200 (crew 1 leader + 6)

entries.desc: Stringers measured from the wharf centerline; toenailed to pile caps with two 3/8 x 10-in spikes at each bearing point; ends overlap for full bearing on caps; spacer blocks toenailed between stringers with two 60d nails. Decking: standard 4x8-in planks spiked to each stringer with two 5/16 x 7-in spikes, 1/4-in spacing (wider in heavy-rain areas). Stringpiece (curb) on 2x10-in blocking 24 in long on 48-in centers along deck edge; bolts countersunk with bituminous-sealed holes; stringpieces parallel to stringers bolted through blocking, decking and stringer end pieces; perpendicular ones bolted through blocking, decking, alternate stringers and pile cap
entries.use: Building the wharf deck
entries.how: Decking 4x8 planks, two 5/16x7-in spikes per stringer, 1/4-in gaps
entries.dim: Stringer spikes 3/8x10 in (2 per bearing); spacers 2x60d; deck 4x8 in planks, 2 spikes 5/16x7 in per stringer, 1/4-in gap; blocking 2x10x24 in at 48 in o.c
entries.tm: Table C-13: stringers 40 MH per 1,000 BF; 4-in deck 20 MH per 1,000 sq ft; bull rail 60 MH per 1,000 linear ft (crew 1 leader + 10)

entries.desc: Fender piles cushion impact, protect bearing piles and hulls; not structural so easier to replace; 3- or 4-ft extension above deck supplements mooring hardware but is not used for warping ships. Driven at a slight batter; usually 1 to 12 fender piles along the outside of bearing-pile rows (except extreme inshore sections); every third fender pile may extend 3-4 ft above the curb, others flush with curb top. Chocks: timber braces between fender piles at stringpiece or cap level, ends firmly seated; on timber-pile wharves each chock fastened with two bolts through stringer end piece or pile cap. Wales: 12x12-in continuous longitudinal timber bolted to the back of each fender pile at mean low water where tidal currents are swift or tide variation great. Protection: wearing ribbon, floating logs/camels, rope wrappings
entries.use: Protecting the wharf from ship impact
entries.how: Fender piles driven at slight batter; every third one extends 3-4 ft above the curb
entries.dim: Every 3rd fender pile extends 3-4 ft above curb; chocks: 2 bolts each; wale 12x12 in at mean low water

entries.n: Pile clusters, corner fenders and dolphins
entries.desc: Clusters (3 or more piles) supplement mooring hardware, top lashed; at most three piles of each cluster extend 3 ft or more above deck. Corner fenders: standard cluster of 10 battered piles bolted and lashed, extending 3 to 4 ft above deck, heavy rope mats lashed at contact level; corner deck reinforced with two layers of plank, each 6 in thick, laid diagonally and transversely, with stringers set close and spiked over the outer half of each corner panel, backed by diagonal batter piles and a diagonal cap bolted to bottom face of other caps. Dolphins: isolated clusters with a king pile (may be a cluster driven vertically and wrapped), other piles battered to the center in concentric rings; king pile left longer for a mooring post; wrap king pile with at least six turns of 1-in galvanized wire rope, stapled to each pile at every turn; two wrappings – one near top and the second about 2/3 of the distance above mean low water; piles chocked and bolted about 2 ft above mean low water. Floating log fenders: logs secured with two or more lengths of 1/2-in galvanized chain to 3/4-in eyebolts; camels are floating clusters/rafts
entries.use: Mooring/fendering where bollards not available; pivoting corners
entries.how: Corner fender = 10 battered piles; dolphin king pile wrapped with 1-in wire rope, 6+ turns
entries.dim: Corner cluster 10 piles; plank layers 2 x 6 in; wire rope 1 in galvanized, >= 6 turns; chain 1/2 in galvanized; eyebolts 3/4 in; chock/bolt 2 ft above MLW

entries.desc: Bollards (single/double bitt) usually designed for line pulls of about 35 tons; corner mooring posts up to 60 tons; cleats for smaller ships/tugs/workboats; open or closed chocks (closed when a line changes both vertical and horizontal direction); pad eyes only for small craft. Stringer reinforcement: base width over 12 and under 24 in -> at least two 12x12 in stringers; over 24 and under 36 in -> three 12x12 in stringers; and so forth; stringers close together, spiked to each other and at bearing points. Standard installations: pier 90x500 ft – six large double-bitt bollards each side on 100-ft centers + five 42-in cleats each side between bollards; offshore marginal wharf 60x500 ft – same on outshore side only; lighterage quay 35x500 ft – eleven 42-in cleats on 50-ft centers. Without cleats/pad eyes extend every third fender pile 3-4 ft above deck (to steady a ship, not winch). Place hardware clear of cranes and traffic, close to curb
entries.use: Selecting and placing docking hardware
entries.how: Bollards ~35 tons; corner posts to 60 tons; increase stringers under heavy hardware
entries.dim: Bollard ~35 tons; corner post up to 60 tons; stringers 12x12 in (2 for 12-24 in base, 3 for 24-36 in); pier 90x500 ft: 6 bollards/side at 100 ft + 5 cleats; quay 35x500 ft: 11 cleats at 50 ft
entries.tm: Table C-14: bits 3 MH each, bollards 4, chocks 3, cleats 2, pad eyes 1 (crew 1 leader + 4)

entries.n: Anchor mooring hardware to the wharf
entries.desc: Between pile bents: grillwork of 12x12 timbers bolted under the pile cap; each of the four piles affected by the upward pull is strapped to the cap with 3 x 3/8-in steel strapping spiked to piles and cap; 12x12 filler blocks centered to receive hardware bolts. Over an outside bearing pile (bolt centers 22 to 26 in): two 12x12 timbers about 20 ft long bolted under the pile cap and to both sides of three piles; 12x12 filler timbers about 4 ft long bolted under the hardware bolt location; three affected piles strapped. Bolt centers over 26 in need wider than 12-in timber, doubled timbers, or placement between bents. Longitudinal diagonal bracing at each bollard from just below the pile caps to about low-water level, bolted to each pile. Light items with bolt centers under 8 in (cleats, chocks, pad eyes) are bolted through stringpiece, blocking, decking and stringer end piece
entries.use: Heavy hardware between bents or over a bearing pile
entries.how: 12x12 grillwork under the cap; 3x3/8-in steel straps on affected piles
entries.dim: Grillwork 12x12; straps 3 x 3/8 in; bolt centers 22-26 in -> two 12x12 about 20 ft + 12x12 fillers about 4 ft; light items bolt centers < 8 in

entries.desc: Appendix C tables C-1 to C-14 give man-hours per unit for rough framing, sheathing/siding, insulation, finish carpentry, doors, flooring, windows, roofing, pile bracing/capping, pier framing and deck hardware, presuming average conditions (weather, skill, crew size, accessibility, equipment). Typical crews: rough framing/trusses 1 leader + 8 (min 1+2); sheathing/siding 1+8; insulation 1+4; finish carpentry 1+3 to 8; flooring 1+4; built-up roofing 1+6; roll roofing 1+6; shingle roofing 1+4; metal/asbestos-cement/tile roofing 1+5; pile bracing/capping 1+6; pier framing 1+10; deck hardware 1+4. Rough framing man-hours per 1,000 BF: beams (3 - 2x8) 30; floor joists, sills 25; wall frames, plates 45; furring incl. plugging 32; blocking 20; ceiling joists 25; rafters 45; bridging 5 per 100 pairs; grounds for plaster 48 per 1,000 linear ft; door bucks 3 each. Insulation per 1,000 sq ft: board floor 32, wall 8, ceiling 24, roof 24; rock wool loose 16, batts 12; foil 8; rigid foam 24; acoustic strip 24, quilt 8
entries.use: Planning crew size and time for carpentry tasks
entries.how: Use the man-hours-per-unit tables; they exclude loading and hauling
entries.dim: See Tables C-1 to C-14
entries.tm: See Table C-1 through C-14 (tables file)
entries.src: TM 3-34.47 Appendix C / Tables C-1 to C-14

entries.desc: For 12-in tiles, floor area in sq ft = number of tiles, plus 10 percent waste. For other sizes: area (sq ft) x 144, divide by tile area (sq in), add 10 percent. Example: 9x9 in tiles, 12 ft x 9 ft room: 108 sq ft x 144 = 15,552 sq in / 81 = 192 tiles + 19 = 211 tiles
entries.use: Ordering tile
entries.how: Area x 144 / tile area in sq in, plus 10 percent waste
entries.dim: Waste 10 percent; example 12x9 ft room with 9x9 in tiles = 211 tiles
entries.tm: Table C-6: soft tile cemented 24 MH per 1,000 sq ft, nailed 32; linoleum 32
entries.src: TM 3-34.47 para D-2, D-3 / Table C-6

entries.desc: Common sizes 9x9 or 12x12 in. Locate center of end walls, snap main centerline, lay a perpendicular centerline (framing square or triangulation); trial layout: if the last tile at the wall is less than 1/2 tile wide move the centerline half a tile toward the wall. Spread adhesive over one quarter of the area at a time starting farthest from the door, up to but not covering chalk lines, using the notch depth the adhesive maker recommends; let it take an initial set. Lay tile from the center, edges on chalk lines, rows stair-stepped, cross-grained pattern; border tiles last (place loose tile over last row grain opposite, mark against wall, cut); remove excess adhesive with approved cleaner
entries.use: Floor finishing
entries.how: Snap centerlines at right angles; shift the line half a tile if border tile would be under half width
entries.dim: Tiles 9x9 or 12x12 in; border tile not narrower than 1/2 tile
entries.eq: Notched trowel, tile cutter, chalk line, framing square

entries.desc: Check the area is square (slightly out can be absorbed in layout; seriously out requires repairs first). Draw layout on paper using as many full tiles and as few cut tiles as possible, cut tiles away from focal points. Snap reference lines for cut-tile perimeter rows and a grid enclosing full tiles in sections no larger than 3 sq ft. Spread adhesive (thinset or organic mastic) on a 3x3 ft section up to the lines; align first tile on a 90-degree grid intersection; use a beating block to level after each course; after the adhesive sets (per manufacturer) spread grout filling joints; clean with damp sponge as grout begins to dry; wipe haze when dry; apply grout sealer after about 72 hours
entries.use: Walls and floors needing sanitary, stain-resistant surface
entries.how: Spread adhesive 3x3 ft at a time; grout cures about 72 hours before sealing
entries.dim: Sections <= 3 sq ft grid; 3x3 ft adhesive area; cure approx 72 hours
entries.eq: Striking tool, beating block, square-notched trowel, pointing trowel, tile cutter, file/tile stone, tile nipper, squeegee/sponge, sponge float, electric tile saw

entries.desc: Acoustical tile 3/16 to 3/4 in thick, 12-30 in wide, 12-60 in long; most common 2x2 and 2x4 ft. Grid: main tee (12-ft), cross tee (2- and 4-ft), wall angle (10-ft), splice plate. Layout: round ceiling length and width up to the next 2-ft multiple (12 ft 7 in x 10 ft 4 in -> 14 x 12 ft); main tees perpendicular to joists; equal, as-large-as-possible border panels; wall angle pieces = perimeter / 10, round up. Mark a level line around the room; minimum 2 in between new and existing ceilings; secure wall angle on the line. Suspension wire 16-gauge annealed every 4 ft along main tees and on each side of splices, cut at least 2 ft longer than the gap between old and new ceilings; hangers: screw eyelets, hooks and nails, 8d common or larger nails bent in a U, Hilti fastener for concrete/steel. Install main tees, then cross tees, then full panels, then border panels
entries.use: Acoustic control, lowering ceilings, covering damaged plaster
entries.how: Layout in 2-ft modules; wire every 4 ft; at least 2 in below the old ceiling
entries.dim: Wire 16-gauge at 4-ft intervals; wire length >= gap + 2 ft; min 2 in clearance to old ceiling; main tee 12 ft, cross tee 2 and 4 ft, wall angle 10 ft
entries.tm: Table C-4: ceilings – panel with suspension 72 MH per 1,000 sq ft
entries.src: TM 3-34.47 para D-20 to D-28 / Table C-4

entries.desc: Tools: 2-4 in wall brush, roller with cover, pan, stepladder, paddle, rags, flat latex paint, bucket of water. Remove paint film, stir thoroughly in figure-8 motion, scrape bottom and sides, fill pan 2/3 full. Ceiling: brush a narrow strip around the perimeter, roll the rest, cross roll to avoid voids. Walls: brush inside corners and corner posts, cut in around trim and baseboards, roll the rest; second coat when first is completely dry. Clean spots with solvent and rag, return excess paint to the can, clean brushes and rollers
entries.use: Final finish
entries.how: Cut in edges with a brush, then roll; fill pan only 2/3
entries.dim: Pan filled 2/3 full
entries.eq: Brush 2-4 in, roller, pan, stepladder, paddle, rags, latex flat paint

entries.desc: Engineering capabilities and activities that directly support maneuver of land combat forces requiring close, integrated support. Enhances friendly mobility and denies enemy mobility by shaping the physical environment
entries.use: Close support to maneuver of land combat forces; only discipline trained and equipped to support movement and maneuver in close combat
entries.how: Combat engineers mainly do mobility, countermobility and survivability (M/CM/S); with tools/training they can also do some general engineering (e.g., improve culverts and fords, repair command posts)
entries.eq: Trained and equipped for close combat; small arms/crew-served weapons (general & geospatial have limited small arms for self-defense)

entries.desc: Most diverse of the three disciplines; may use all engineer MOSs. One of the Army logistics elements: establishes and maintains infrastructure to conduct and sustain operations
entries.use: Provide infrastructure and modify, maintain or protect the physical environment; construction support across all levels of warfare and every operation type
entries.how: Common tasks: restore damaged areas; build/maintain LOCs; establish base camps; assess/repair infrastructure; environmental surveys/reports; hazmat/waste infrastructure; master facility/design support; electrical power generation/distribution; real estate acquisition/disposal

entries.desc: Supports all warfighting functions through terrain analysis and visualization via the Army Geospatial Enterprise (AGE); data held in Theater Geospatial Database (TGD), ASCC geospatial planning cells, Army Geospatial Center
entries.use: Provide geospatial information and services (GI&S) so commanders/staffs understand the physical environment; supports running estimates and decisions
entries.how: Four primary functions: generate, manage, analyze, disseminate (GMAD). Support from ASCC to BCT includes terrain analysis, 3-D terrain visualization, tailored map products (cross-country mobility, view shed, zone of entry, hydrology), SSGF data for the COP, and TGD maintenance

entries.desc: Orchestrates combat, general and geospatial engineering in combination
entries.use: Gain/maintain a position of advantage (mobility) and deny the enemy freedom of action (countermobility); supports movement and maneuver, incl. special operations forces
entries.how: Achieved through the assured mobility framework (ATP 3-90.4). Normally organic combat engineers; general engineers may be task-organized. Does not include nontactical movement of personnel/material for logistics

entries.desc: Combination of the three disciplines supporting force preservation
entries.use: Preserve the force so commanders can apply maximum combat power
entries.how: Largely survivability operations, but can include selected mobility (e.g., perimeter roads), countermobility (protective obstacles) and explosive-hazards tasks (area clearance)

entries.n: Line of Support: Enable Force Projection and Logistics
entries.desc: Often performed by engineer units or contract construction (e.g., USACE) and may combine joint units, contractors, HN or multinational engineers
entries.use: Enhance theater strategic-to-tactical movements; executed mainly by general engineering
entries.how: Tasks free combat engineers for maneuver, build/maintain infrastructure for follow-on forces, sustain operations during/after hostile action, recommend site selection for facilities, joint fires and protection

entries.n: Line of Support: Build Partner Capacity and Develop Infrastructure
entries.desc: Primarily general engineering; also uses geospatial engineers and USACE experts for technical advice and data exchange
entries.use: Stability and counterinsurgency tasks; building/repairing infrastructure, essential services, and co-developing HN capability
entries.how: Purpose differs from logistics: e.g., a road for the local economy may prioritize local labor/ coordination/ training HN managers over speed. USACE FFE units advise HN capacity building; BCT engineers may provide training or reconstruction teams

entries.desc: Combat engineers usually at tactical level in support of maneuver; general engineers typically at operational level. Road/bridge/airfield repair is usually general engineering
entries.use: Mitigate effects of natural and man-made obstacles so friendly forces can move and maneuver freely
entries.how: Five primary tasks: combined arms breaching; clearing (areas and routes); gap crossing; construct/maintain combat roads and trails; construct/maintain forward airfields and landing zones. Also bypass, reduce or clear obstacles and mark lanes and trails

entries.desc: Combat engineers play prominent tactical role; general engineers may support operational/strategic effects or deception. In stability, may support traffic/population control
entries.use: Use or enhance natural/man-made obstacles to prevent enemy freedom of movement and maneuver; shape enemy movement; isolate objectives in the offense
entries.how: Tasks: siting obstacles; constructing, emplacing or detonating obstacles; marking, reporting and recording obstacles; maintaining obstacle integration. Engineer advises commander on integration, coordinates obstacle emplacement authority, establishes obstacle control, supervises employment, tracks status; plans to clear obstacles at end of hostilities
entries.wn: As of 1 Jan 2010 U.S. forces may not employ persistent, undetectable land mines; self-destructing/self-deactivating (scatterable) mines and networked munitions are used. Follow current U.S. land mine policy

entries.desc: Geospatial engineers work as staff members supporting the orders process and the COP
entries.use: Help combat/general engineers visualize the operational environment for mobility tasks
entries.how: Products: 3-D fly-throughs; mobility corridor and combined obstacle overlays; fields-of-fire/line-of-sight analysis; urban tactical planners; hydrologic/bathymetric/gravimetric analysis; LOC analysis and overlays

entries.desc: Equipment and personnel to conduct underwater operations (see ATP 3-34.84, TM 3-34.84). Integrate into early-entry operations and port opening
entries.use: Underwater operations; river-crossing support and force protection dives
entries.how: Provides near-shore/far-shore recon; hydrographic surveys of bottom composition; underwater/surface recon of bridges for structural integrity; repair/reinforce bridge structures; emplace, mark or reduce underwater obstacles; check ships, docks, piers, intakes for enemy tampering; identify/remove underwater explosive hazards
entries.eq: Diving detachment equipment and personnel (details in ATP 3-34.84 / TM 3-34.84, not in this source)

entries.desc: Formed by combat engineer units. See ATP 3-34.81
entries.use: Classify routes, locate obstacles, recommend bypass or reduction; recon proposed obstacle locations
entries.how: Normally supports BCTs, cavalry squadrons or scout platoons; can operate independently. Submit all terrain, obstacle and recon data to geospatial engineers to update the COP and TGD. Teams are ad hoc, so building them from organic resources drains platoons/squads
entries.wn: Ad hoc formations; commanders must understand the risk of drawing from organic platoons and squads (para 2-106)

entries.desc: Limited to ordnance in the EOCA guide or supplemental EOCA ordnance list
entries.use: Limited disposal of authorized explosive ordnance in support of mobility; advise on protective measures
entries.how: Combat engineers with extra training; advise on-scene commander on personnel/equipment protective measures; isolate blast and fragmentation danger areas; may assist EOD
entries.wn: Only authorized ordnance on EOCA list; EOD assist as directed by theater

entries.desc: Tactical level: usually combat engineers in support of maneuver; operational level: general engineers. Protective positions and hardened facilities also support protection against nuclear blast and improve shielding in CBRN environments; engineers support decontamination sites and scrape roads/surfaces to reduce contamination
entries.use: Alter the physical environment to provide or improve cover, concealment and camouflage when terrain is insufficient
entries.how: Four areas: fighting positions, protective positions, hardened facilities, camouflage and concealment. Tasks are equipment-intensive; use equipment timelines to manage low-density critical equipment. See ATP 3-37.34 for details
entries.eq: Dig assets and other engineer equipment (not itemized)

entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.20
entries.use: Mitigate effects of explosive hazards at all echelons
entries.how: Includes area and route clearance; specialized searches using engineer mine detection dogs and patrol explosive detection dogs; collection, analysis, dissemination of explosive hazard information. Where tactical situation permits, area clearance can be a USACE-contracted capability
entries.eq: Mine detection dogs, patrol explosive detection dogs
entries.wn: Area clearance is not demining; 10 USC 401 Chapter 20 restricts armed forces from demining unless supporting a U.S. military operation

entries.n: Protective Obstacles and Entry Control Points (perimeter protection)
entries.desc: See ADP 3-37
entries.use: Protect bases and base camps
entries.how: Examples: construct a trail for use as a perimeter road to secure a base; provide protective obstacles or entry control points

entries.desc: Limited-asset teams
entries.use: Fire prevention and protection (limited assets)
entries.how: Fire prevention inspections/investigations, fire suppression, search and rescue, hazmat response, medical response/assistance to victims, technical oversight of nonfirefighting personnel supporting firefighting

entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.5, AR 200-1
entries.use: Identify, prevent and mitigate hazards to the environment, personnel and mission before force projection and site occupation
entries.how: Embedded engineers conduct environmental baseline surveys, analyze site conditions, identify resources/hazards, recommend actions. Records during contingency location life cycle: Environmental Baseline Survey Checklists and Reports, Environmental Conditions Reports, inspection reports, Environmental Site Closure Surveys and Reports. Example site problems: poor drainage, contaminated soil, poor water/air quality, erosion, flooding, over-stacked/leaking hazmat containers, improper waste

entries.n: Route Reconnaissance and Clearance for Force Projection
entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.81
entries.use: Determine trafficability and route classification; clear hazards for freedom of movement along LOC, APOD or SPOD
entries.how: Combat engineers conduct route recon; detect/mark explosive hazards; clear hazards within capability

entries.use: Port facilities unavailable, damaged or denied
entries.how: Engineers augment sustainment units; prepare access routes to/from beach; prepare landing sites and staging areas

entries.n: General Engineering Task List (construction and sustainment)
entries.desc: See ATP 3-34.40
entries.use: Primarily not under close-combat conditions
entries.how: Construct/maintain strategic and operational LOCs, airfields, seaports, railroads, bases/base camps, pipelines, bulk and distribution storage facilities, standard and nonstandard bridges; facilities engineer support; electrical power generation/distribution; utilities and waste; real estate; firefighting; battle damage repair; environmental surveys/reports; improving fighting/protective positions and hardening facilities; Corps real estate teams; engineer divers; neutralize water-borne obstacles in ports/channels; repair/reinforce subsurface structures (port facilities, dams, bridges); search and recovery of submerged equipment; JLOTS support

entries.n: Well Drilling and Water Source Mapping
entries.use: Long-term water restoration issues
entries.how: Specialized units can locate and map water sources; well-drilling teams are limited assets

entries.use: Describe the OE with eight operational variables: political, military, economic, social, information, infrastructure, physical environment, time
entries.how: Engineer view adds items such as port access, enemy explosive hazards, availability of materials, laborers and local engineer resources, power considerations, infrastructure deficiencies, urban/complex terrain, and base camp permanence vs duration

entries.desc: Early identification of essential engineer tasks lets the maneuver commander request augmentation early
entries.use: Mission analysis for a specific operation
entries.how: Mission; Enemy (disposition, enemy engineering capabilities, obstacle intelligence, recon, explosive hazard reporting); Terrain and weather (five military aspects: observation and fields of fire, avenues of approach, key terrain, obstacles, cover and concealment); Troops and support available; Time available; Civil considerations; (Informational considerations)

entries.desc: Special operations forces support: engineer LNO integrated into SOF HQ; contingency/crisis action planning; speed and resource ingenuity
entries.use: Link tactical actions to national objectives
entries.how: National strategic (policy); theater strategic (force planning, GI&S, TGD, SPOD/APOD, LOCs, basing, joint targeting, foreign humanitarian assistance, environmental, explosive hazard mitigation); operational (base camp site selection, supply routes, waste programs, Class IV procurement, environment); tactical (task-organize engineers at lowest level, survivability and infrastructure; geospatial engineers validate recon data and submit to TGD)

entries.use: Small UASs make suppression/obscuration for breach or gap crossing harder, and can observe survivability work and pinpoint battle positions
entries.how: Commanders account for enemy capabilities and implement counter-small-UAS techniques based on organic and attached capabilities; Soldiers must be trained and equipped (see ATP 3-01.81)

entries.n: Engineer support across strategic contexts (competition, crisis, armed conflict)
entries.use: Engineer demand remains high from competition through armed conflict
entries.how: Competition: geospatial and general engineering tasks, theater setting, partner capacity. Crisis: real estate/basing, opening ports of debarkation, LOCs, hardening facilities, AAs/battle positions; reserve component mobilization time matters (about three-fourths of Army engineer units are in the reserve component). Armed conflict: support to ground combat and sustainment

entries.desc: Supporting orgs: theater engineer command (TEC) and USACE. See ATP 3-37.10 (base camps), ATP 3-37.34
entries.use: Establish favorable conditions for rapid execution of operations for a specific OPLAN
entries.how: Infrastructure improvement; bases and base camp planning; APOD/SPOD hardening; surveys of assembly areas, LOC capacity, gap-crossing sites; real estate; environmental services. Manage Class IV (barrier/construction) and Class V (explosives) supply separately

entries.use: Evaluate whether infrastructure meets operational needs
entries.how: Questions: meets needs over campaign phases (quantity, quality, location, force protection)? meets coalition/HN needs? repair/upgrade/maintain/new construction? defense/protection needs? is it on the critical, defended or protection prioritization list? FEST-A provides infrastructure assessment

entries.desc: Defense demands the greatest survivability effort (HQ, artillery, air and missile defense, critical equipment/supplies, individual/crew-served and defilade vehicle positions). Use engineer work timelines; digging assets are intensively managed
entries.use: Defeat enemy attack, gain time, develop conditions for offense/stability
entries.how: Engineer focus: combined-arms obstacle integration (countermobility), survivability of defending force, and assured mobility for repositioning/counterattacking forces. Combat engineers: construct field fortifications and fighting positions, combat roads, FACE, obstacles, demolitions, place mines/munitions, recon, fight as engineers/infantry. General: harden facilities, horizontal construction, support CM/S, mitigate hazards, protect water supplies, environmental. Geospatial: terrain analysis of EAs, SSGF for COP
entries.eq: Digging assets, barrier materials, munitions, construction equipment (not itemized)
entries.wn: Countermobility efforts compete with survivability resources and assets; commander must give clear priorities (note after para 2-62)

entries.desc: Link obstacles to restrictive/natural terrain. See ATP 3-90.8
entries.use: Mass effects to contain and destroy an enemy force
entries.how: Seven steps: identify likely enemy AAs; identify most likely enemy COA; determine where to kill the enemy; *position subordinate forces and weapons; *plan and integrate obstacles; *plan and integrate fires; rehearse (*simultaneous). Obstacle siting is a support rehearsal: walk the terrain with the supported maneuver unit to ensure fires cover the EA. Obstacle options: networked munitions, scatterable mines, demolition obstacles (road craters), constructed obstacles, field expedient obstacles

entries.desc: Mobile defense generally needs less engineer effort than area defense
entries.use: Destroy enemy through decisive attack by striking force/mobile reserve
entries.how: Use obstacles to defeat enemy maneuver; give mobility to striking force; situational obstacles advantageous; primary and alternate hull-defilade positions in primary and subsequent battle positions; protective obstacles concentrated at final subsequent positions; obstacle control measures so brigade obstacles do not limit the reserve; dedicated engineer support to the mobile reserve

entries.desc: Area defense generally requires more robust engineer effort due to higher survivability requirement
entries.use: Deny enemy access to terrain for a specific time; retain terrain
entries.how: Variations: defense of a linear obstacle, perimeter defense, reverse slope defense. Brigades may need primary, alternate and supplementary turret-defilade positions; heavier protective obstacles; coordinate adjacent brigade obstacle efforts; scatterable mines allow less risk

entries.use: Organized movement away from the enemy (delay, withdrawal, retirement)
entries.how: Maintain mobility of force (disengagement of force in contact) and protect the force; normally under limited visibility; hinder enemy mobility with obstacles, fires, and terrain optimization

entries.use: Authority to emplace reinforcing obstacles
entries.how: Delegated: theater commanders -> corps commanders -> division commanders; division commanders retain unless higher commander withholds/restricts

entries.desc: Position engineers well forward; keep task organization changes minimal (time/event-based triggers). Fighting/protective position development is minimal in offense; CPs and key assets need improved survivability on halts
entries.use: Defeat/destroy enemy forces and gain control of terrain, resources, population centers
entries.how: Priority: mobility. Combat: breach obstacles, demolitions, clear explosive hazards, field fortifications, assault bridging, combat roads, FACE, recon. General: port construction, horizontal construction, quarry aggregate, asphalt, concrete, underwater construction, firefighting. Geospatial: terrain analysis of assembly areas and objectives. Prefer bypass; mark bypasses and hand off to follow-on engineers; LOC bridging replaces assault bridging

entries.n: Engineer considerations by offensive operation type
entries.use: Movement to contact, attack, exploitation, pursuit
entries.how: See Table 2-3

entries.desc: See ATP 3-90.4
entries.use: Allow maneuver through an obstacle covered by enemy fire
entries.how: Synchronized combined arms activity under maneuver commander control; breaching tenets: intelligence, breaching fundamentals, breaching organization, mass, synchronization; rehearse breach, assault and support forces; engineers reduce, mark and guide units through obstacles; corps units expand lanes and breach bypassed obstacles

entries.use: Eliminate enemy obstacle effects or residual obstacles affecting a route or area
entries.how: Clearance teams task-organized and rehearsed; area clearance organized so sustainment assets can echelon forward

entries.use: Project combat power across a wet or dry gap
entries.how: Fundamentals: surprise; extensive preparation (less for hasty); flexible planning; traffic management; organization; speed. Requires specialized crossing resources and a force to secure the bridgehead. Corps bridging provides assault float bridging and LOC bridging

entries.n: Construct and Maintain Combat Roads and Trails
entries.use: Move personnel/equipment/supplies through untrafficable areas and bypass obstacles or sensitive areas
entries.how: Combat engineering mission in close support; general engineers also build them. Corps units upgrade combat roads and trails

entries.use: Hasty construction/repair of landing strips, landing zones, forward arming and refueling points
entries.how: Shortens distance to objective areas, reduces turnaround times, improves sustainment for fixed-, rotary-, tilt-wing aircraft (manned/unmanned)

entries.use: Improve trafficability and movement
entries.how: Repair and clear roads; traffic pattern studies; design/install permanent traffic control devices (technical expertise)

entries.desc: Technical expertise often through reachback or forward USACE contingency element
entries.use: Secure environment, essential services, emergency reconstruction, humanitarian relief
entries.how: Six primary stability tasks; essential services: food and water, emergency shelter, basic sanitation. General engineering: harden facilities, horizontal/vertical construction, LOC construction and repair, infrastructure, waste, well drilling, quarry, asphalt, concrete, power, utilities, survey and design, construction management, firefighting. Early on-ground assessment tailors force. Contract capabilities (LOGCAP, AFCAP, NAVFAC GCCC) take over as AO matures

entries.use: Make operational success enduring
entries.how: Assess civil infrastructure; area clearance; recon LOCs/roads/bridges; improve force protection for critical infrastructure; improve combat roads and replace tactical bridging with LOC bridging; contract Class IV and equipment/labor; assess/document environmental conditions; construct base camps

entries.use: Transitions can be chaotic and increase risk
entries.how: Anticipate and plan deliberately; consolidate gains facilitates transition

entries.use: Urban operations and sharing GD&I
entries.how: ATP 3-06 urban framework: understand, shape, engage, consolidate, transition. Geospatial engineers partner with local authorities to share GD&I; support SSGF; GEOINT cells

entries.use: Many threats/non-state actors do not mark mines doctrinally
entries.how: Learn local marking methods (readily available materials); consult local authorities about natural, cultural, historic resources and sensitive populations

entries.desc: Smaller multifunctional elements
entries.use: Engineer support at company, platoon, squad or Soldier level
entries.how: GI&S, infrastructure development, facility construction/maintenance, training indigenous populations to construct protective obstacles, mobile electric power, facility hardening

entries.n: Support to Cyberspace Operations and Electromagnetic Warfare
entries.use: Protect cyber-dependent operations
entries.how: Harden facilities; construct protective obstacles; provide uninterrupted medium-voltage power; clean/secure power supply and grid systems to mitigate electromagnetic disruption

entries.n: Host-Nation Support and Engineer Support Plan (ESP)
entries.desc: Wartime HN support agreements exist in Europe and Korea
entries.use: Reduce early lift requirements for RSOI
entries.how: JCMS planning module identifies construction requirements; USACE Centers of Standardization site-adapt drawings; analyses produce the ESP (see para 6-28). HN may provide geospatial data, land, facilities, construction support, manpower, equipment, materials, services, waste disposal. Pre-position equipment regionally; HN local contractors and materials (cement, asphalt, aggregate, lumber, steel)

entries.use: Unity of effort with joint, multinational, interagency, NGOs
entries.how: Provide engineer LNOs (linguist, communications, transport); request HN geospatial data; use ATP 3-34 / ATP-3.12.1 for allied engineers; establish liaison with civil-military operations center; NGOs may be Class IV source

entries.n: Engineer Support at Echelon (Theater Army, Corps, Division, BCT)
entries.use: Understand who does what by echelon
entries.how: Theater army: infrastructure assessment, basing, set the theater, RSOI. Corps: base camp planning, geospatial products, recon, joint fires and survivability recommendations; corps normally has an engineer brigade HQ. Division: up to five BCTs; division engineers integrate combat, general and geospatial support. BCT: divisionally aligned engineer battalion/BEB provides baseline combat capability; BCT HQ has geospatial engineers in the intelligence section

entries.n: Engineer Support Across the Six Warfighting Functions
entries.desc: Six warfighting functions: C2, movement and maneuver, intelligence, fires, sustainment, protection. Engineer disciplines are organized by discipline and synchronized through these functions (Figure 3-1)
entries.use: Linking engineer disciplines to the warfighting functions so engineer capability is applied as combat power
entries.how: Know which discipline mainly feeds which function: combat engineering -> movement and maneuver + protection; general engineering -> sustainment (secondary: protection); geospatial -> C2 (liaison to intelligence); survivability links to fires + protection
entries.eq: Combat, general and geospatial engineer units

entries.n: Engineer C2 Support (Command and Control WFF)
entries.desc: Engineer units integrate the operations process activities with the supported unit (through assigned engineer staff or staff counterparts). Engineer headquarters control ongoing engineer operations: monitoring engineer forces/assets, mitigating explosive hazards, coordinating engineer reconnaissance, and providing geospatial support through GI&S
entries.use: Engineer units integrate with the supported unit's operations process; prioritizing scarce engineer capability
entries.how: Prioritize carefully because there are usually not enough engineer capabilities; expect to shift capabilities within the AO as mission changes; use mission command approach

entries.desc: A graphic control measure: a coordinated boundary or phase line used to compartmentalize an AO and designate areas of work responsibility for subordinate engineer organizations
entries.use: Designate which engineer unit has primary responsibility for engineer effort in part of the AO
entries.how: Used at division level to separate an AO supported by division engineer assets from an AO supported by direct/general support corps engineer units
entries.eq: Graphic control measure on operations graphics

entries.desc: Engineers support movement and maneuver through geospatial engineering, engineer reconnaissance, and M/CM/S. Combat engineer support is focused on assured mobility
entries.use: Combat engineers support forces in close combat; shape the battlefield for early-entry operations
entries.how: Support assured mobility; BCT organic and divisionally aligned engineers use mobility and countermobility tasks to enable and expand lodgments
entries.eq: BCT organic and divisionally aligned engineer units

entries.desc: Combat engineers can perform as general engineers (and vice versa) only with additional equipment, training and augmented technical expertise. General engineer units tasked in support of maneuver forces are closer to the front than usual; without maneuver security they must self-secure, which pulls personnel from the task and extends time on site
entries.use: Close combat support to maneuver forces
entries.how: Integrate and coordinate with fire and movement of combat forces. Combat engineer units are organized like infantry squads/platoons with extra medical personnel, specific weapons and vehicles, trained with supported forces
entries.eq: Combat engineer units; general engineers need augmentation/security
entries.wn: General engineers lack the same weapon types as combat engineers, increasing risk to personnel and equipment (para 3-15)

entries.desc: Close-combat engineer tasks: neutralize explosive hazards (locate, assess, render incapable of interfering; except render-safe); enhance mobility (route and obstacle reconnaissance, obstacle reduction, assault gap crossing, combat roads and trails, forward aviation combat engineering); deny enemy movement (land mines, network munitions, demolition and constructed obstacles); enhance protection through survivability (fighting and protective positions, hardening, camouflage and concealment)
entries.use: Combat engineers engage in close combat to accomplish engineer missions
entries.how: Be prepared to fight and integrate with fire and maneuver; the enemy tries to detect and engage engineers quickly regardless of location
entries.eq: Land mines, network munitions, demolitions, constructed obstacles (as listed)

entries.desc: A combat engineer organization can execute infantry tasks or task-organize to fight as infantry. The combat engineer unit commander has authority to reorganize unless reserved; must weigh gain in infantry strength against loss of engineer support
entries.use: Rare: engineer unit designated to fight as infantry
entries.how: Requires added fire support and medical positions; decision normally made at operational-level command and coordinated with higher HQ. An immediate need may only require engineers to engage in close combat without reorganizing
entries.eq: Extensive equipment and training specific to reorganization
entries.wn: Reorganization requires resources, time and training; employing engineers merely means short-term use (para 3-18)

entries.n: General Engineer Support to Movement and Maneuver
entries.desc: General engineer support is typically applied through sustainment but crosses over to movement and maneuver
entries.use: Tasks exceeding combat engineer capability; major upgrades or new construction of LOCs and base camps
entries.how: Examples listed: roads/trails beyond combat engineer capability, runway repair, airfield surveys, firefighting and aircraft rescue, marking airfield surfaces, field-expedient landing strips, standard and nonstandard bridging, theater access (LOCs, MSRs, ports, airfields, base camps)

entries.n: Intelligence WFF Support / Engineer IPOE Support
entries.desc: Engineers play a major role in IPOE supporting G-2/S-2 and G-3/S-3 analysis. Geospatial engineering improves terrain visualization and provides SSGF to GEOINT
entries.use: Adds to commander's situational understanding of terrain, weather, civil considerations
entries.how: Provide digitized mapping and terrain analysis; predictive and deductive analysis of enemy engineering capabilities; civil infrastructure considerations (PMESII-PT); support information collection through engineer reconnaissance

entries.desc: A deliberate process. Engineer information requirements are determined by engineer staffs at division, corps, theater army and in-theater engineer HQs in coordination with the G-2
entries.use: Determine feasibility of areas for use; assess AO before and during deployment
entries.how: Collect remotely or physically; may include conditions/capacities supporting mobility, sources of construction materials, local construction standards, key industrial sites, cultural heritage sites, geotechnical data (soils, geology, hydrography). Feed the COP continuously
entries.eq: Engineer staffs; remote or physical collection means

entries.desc: Engineer disciplines provide a menu of reconnaissance capabilities. Units do not have dedicated reconnaissance elements (except the armored BCT). See ATP 3-34.81
entries.use: Answer commander's critical information requirements; support the lines of engineer support
entries.how: Reconnaissance is inherent in all three disciplines; information may be tactical or technical. Commanders task-organize combat and general engineers with other disciplines based on mission
entries.eq: Mix of engineer specialties and equipment

entries.desc: Engineer reconnaissance teams are composed of combat engineers
entries.use: Collect tactical and technical information for M/CM/S: division's freedom of maneuver and survivability of friendly forces and facilities
entries.how: Engineer company commanders form and train ad hoc teams for tactical reconnaissance that collect technical information and perform limited analysis

entries.desc: Engineers complete EBS to record detailed environmental conditions. See ATP 3-34.5
entries.use: Record and analyze environmental conditions to judge whether areas are feasible for use
entries.how: Records hazardous materials, spills/contamination, disease vectors and pests, poor drainage and erosion, natural resources, cultural and historic resources. DD Form 2993 (EBS Checklist) is used to verify and record technical information

entries.desc: GI&S is collection, information extraction, storage, dissemination and exploitation of geodetic, geomagnetic, imagery, gravimetric, aeronautical, topographic, hydrographic, littoral, cultural and toponymic data referenced to a precise location
entries.use: Terrain visualization and understanding for planning, training and operations
entries.how: Common applications: planning, training, terrain visualization, navigation, mission planning, mission rehearsal, modeling, simulation, targeting. AGC reachback provides instruction, training and guidance on using geospatial data
entries.eq: Geospatial engineering teams; Army Geospatial Enterprise (AGE); AGC

entries.desc: At division and above, engineer targets enter the Army targeting process/joint targeting cycle; shift terrain-shaping obstacle systems during dynamic targeting (ATP 3-60.1). Staff planners also protect infrastructure from friendly targeting for future use
entries.use: Facilitate targeting and artillery displacement
entries.how: Geospatial engineers: templated observer and firing points from line-of-sight and slope; mobility/suitability analysis of targets and EAs. Combat engineers: emplace obstacles that enhance fires, construct survivability positions for fires units, support mobility during displacement
entries.wn: Damage to enemy critical infrastructure (airfields, roads, bridges, intersections, yards) may need significant engineer effort to restore for friendly use (para 3-29)

entries.desc: Sustainment elements: logistics, financial management, personnel services, health service support. Engineers support through mobility and survivability tasks
entries.use: Base camps, ammunition holding areas, revetments/hardening of distribution facilities, clearing and repairing LOCs
entries.how: In stability and DSCA, general engineering effort (incl. USACE) is very high at onset then decreases; may transfer to external support contracts (LOGCAP, AFCAP, NAVFAC global contingency construction contract). Operational contract support: general engineers give subject-matter expertise to oversee contracted services and materials

entries.desc: Tasks: vehicle, crew-served and individual fighting positions; protective earth walls, berms, revetments, protective positions for vehicles, information systems, equipment and material; hardening of structures with overhead cover, pre-detonation screens, shielding barriers; bridge protective devices (against waterborne demolition teams, floating mines, debris); install/remove protective obstacles; protective equipment (vehicle crash barriers, entry control points, security fences); environmental baseline surveys
entries.use: Protect the force from enemy action in the AO; hardening and field fortification
entries.how: Combat engineers typically provide basic hardening and field fortification; general engineers focus on long-term survivability, pollution/hazmat control, and facility hardening. See ATP 3-37.34
entries.eq: Engineer equipment and personnel; barriers, fences, bridge protective devices (as listed)

entries.n: CBRN Contamination Control and Firefighting (Protection Tasks)
entries.desc: Listed as engineer protection tasks
entries.use: Control CBRN contamination; fire protection
entries.how: Engineers identify, prevent and mitigate hazards to environment, personnel and mission; see ATP 3-11.33 (CBRN) and TM 3-34.30 (firefighting)

entries.desc: Engineer operations contribute lethal and nonlethal combat power. Corps, divisions and BCTs are task organized with engineer capabilities based on mission variables: platoon, company, battalion or brigade HQ
entries.use: Understanding how engineers contribute to combat power
entries.how: Five dynamics: leadership, firepower, information, mobility, survivability. Survivability is how hard a formation is to kill; includes avoiding detection and deceiving the enemy

entries.n: Lethal and Nonlethal Actions / Shift to Stability
entries.desc: Lethal and nonlethal actions complement each other and create dilemmas for the opponent; nonlethal action denies the enemy a propaganda tool where lethal force is counterproductive
entries.use: Choosing mix of lethal/nonlethal action; stability operations focus
entries.how: In stability operations, building partner capacity and developing infrastructure become the primary line of engineer support: build/repair/maintain infrastructure, provide essential services, codevelop HN capabilities

entries.n: Engineer Regiment and Operating-Force Engineer Categories
